author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. No sooner does such a gentleman make his appearance, than the neighbourhood is united in this belief.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters, with no more concern for his own inclinations than if he were a piece of fine furniture.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: “My dear Mr. Bennet,” said his lady to him one day, bustling into the room with an air of great importance, “have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last? I assure you it is true!”

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Mr. Bennet, who possessed a remarkable talent for remaining completely unruffled by his wife's excitements, merely replied that he had not.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: “But it is,” returned she, her voice rising in her eagerness; “for Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it. You must believe me, for she had it from the best authority.”

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Mr. Bennet made no answer, finding silence to be the most effective counter to his wife's conversational volleys.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: “Do you not want to know who has taken it?” cried his wife impatiently, unable to bear the suspense of his absolute indifference a moment longer.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: “You want to tell me, my dear,” he replied with the utmost composure, “and I have no objection to hearing it, provided it gives you pleasure to speak.”

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: This was invitation enough. A very little encouragement always sufficed for Mrs. Bennet when she was entirely resolved to speak.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: “Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it, that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately. He is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week.”
